deep.reconstruction:
Context. The page continues the previous folio's table 'Pars 2. Primi formae 8n+5'. For each prime p ≡ 5 (mod 8), Gauss tabulates the classes of positive binary quadratic forms of determinant -p (modern discriminant -4p).

Notation. The heading 'p   0,h' gives the class number h. h is the label of the last class plus one; for example 149 has classes 0..13, so h = 14. Gauss evidently writes the class group as cyclic, with classes numbered by powers of a generator. 'C. k.(h-k)' groups class k with its inverse (opposite) class h-k. 'c.' (continet) lists some primes represented by that class. For every even-numbered class, i.e. every class of the principal genus, he writes a representation p = a^2+b^2+c^2.

Why the even classes. The principal genus consists of the squares of classes, which here are the even powers. It has h/2 classes, giving (h/2+1)/2 pairs {k, -k}. These pairs correspond one-to-one to the essentially distinct (up to order and sign) representations of p as a sum of three squares (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, arts. 278-292). Class 0 gets the representation containing a zero, p = a^2 + b^2. The ambiguous class h/2 (odd, since h ≡ 2 mod 4 here) is (2,1,(p+1)/2) and 'contains 2'.

Lines on the page.
- Top left, end of p = 109 (h = 6): C.2.4: 109 = 64+36+9, contains 5. C.3: contains 2.
- p = 149, h = 14:
  - C.0: 149 = 100+49.
  - C.1.13: contains 3. Generator (3,1,50) in Gauss's (a,b,c) with b^2-ac = -149.
  - C.2.12: 149 = 81+64+4.
  - C.3.11: no prime listed.
  - C.4.10: 149 = 144+4+1, contains 5.
  - C.5.9: no prime listed.
  - C.6.8: 149 = 64+49+36.
  - C.7: contains 2.
- p = 157, h = 6: C.0: 121+36. C.1.5. C.2.4: 144+9+4, contains 13, 17. C.3: contains 2, 79, via the form (2,1,79).
- p = 173, h = 14 (continues in the top-right box):
  - C.0: 169+4, contains 1. C.1.13: contains 3.
  - C.2.12: 100+64+9. C.3.11.
  - C.4.10: 121+36+16, contains 13. C.5.9.
  - C.6.8: 144+25+4. C.7: contains 2.
- p = 181, h = 10: C.0: 100+81, contains 1. C.1.9: contains 7. C.2.8: 144+36+1, contains 5. C.3.7. C.4.6: 81+64+36. C.5: contains 2.
- p = 197, h = 10: C.0: 196+1, contains 1. C.1.9: contains 3. C.2.8: 100+81+16. C.3.7. C.4.6: 144+49+4. C.5: contains 2 and 103, since (2,1,99) gives 2+2+99 = 103.
- p = 229, h = 10: C.0: 225+4. C.1.9: contains 7. C.2.8: 144+49+36, contains 5. C.3.7. Continued on the next folio.

My reconstruction of the class attached to a representation. For p = a^2+b^2+c^2 with (a,b,c) primitive, take the rank-2 lattice orthogonal to (a,b,c) in Z^3. Its Gram matrix has determinant p and gives a binary form of determinant -p. I verified that this reproduces Gauss's class labels in every case I tested.
- p = 149, (9,8,2): orthogonal basis (0,1,-4), (2,0,-9); Gram (17,36,85); reduces to (9,-2,17) = (3,1,50)^2, which is class 2.
- p = 149, (12,2,1): gives (5,-1,30) = (3,1,50)^4, which is class 4 and contains 5.
- p = 149, (8,7,6): gives (6,-1,25), class 6.
- p = 173, (10,8,3): Gram (9,-22,73), reduces to (9,-4,21) = (3,1,58)^2, class 2.
- p = 173, (11,6,4): Gram (54,23,13), reduces to (13,-3,14) = (3,1,58)^4, class 4, containing 13.
- p = 109, (8,6,3): gives (5,1,22), class 2, containing 5.
- p = 157, (12,3,2): gives (13,5,14), class 2, containing 13 and 17.

Counting check. The number of three-square representations matches r3(p) = 12 h(-4p) throughout: h = 14 for 149 and 173; h = 10 for 181, 197 and 229; h = 6 for 109 and 157.

The 'contains' entries are consistent with genus characters: (q/p) = +1 for primes in even classes and -1 for primes in odd classes. However, the lists are not exhaustive, and the selection criterion is unclear to me. Examples: 17 is represented in class 2 for 149 and 7 in class 1 for 157, but neither is listed.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. All sums of three squares are correct, the class numbers match r3(p) = 12h(-4p), and the class assignments I tested agree with composition.

The 'c.' (continet) lists are incomplete. Examples: 17 (represented by (9,2,17), class 2 of 149), 11 (an odd class of 149), 7 ((7,2,23), class 1 of 157) and 13 (principal genus of 181) are omitted. This looks like a selection rather than an error.

results.what: Correspondence between essentially distinct representations of a prime p ≡ 5 (mod 8) as a sum of three squares and pairs of opposite classes in the principal genus of forms of determinant -p, with class 0 ↔ p = a^2 + b^2.
results.modern_name: Gauss's three-squares theorem / class-number formula r3(p) = 12 h(-4p); orthogonal-lattice (ternary-to-binary) correspondence

results.what: Cyclic labelling of the class group of determinant -p by powers of a generator; principal genus = even powers (squares); ambiguous class (2,1,(p+1)/2) at position h/2.
results.modern_name: Structure of the form class group, genus theory, principal genus = squares (duplication theorem)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), arts. 286-287 and sec. V generally

results.what: Explicit identification of which class (as a power of the generator) belongs to each three-square representation, numerically tabulated.
results.modern_name: Explicit Gauss correspondence / class of the orthogonal lattice of a primitive vector
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (theory in DA); such tables are part of his Nachlass computations

deep.surprise_reason: This is a computational table applying the theory of DA sec. V (class groups, genera, sums of three squares) that Gauss published in 1801. Specifying the class index of each representation is a nice unpublished detail but entirely within known Gaussian theory.

The top-right lines 'C.6.8. 144+25+4. c.' and 'C.7. c. 2.' belong to the entry for 173 (continued from the bottom of the left column). They are not a separate entry.
The top-left lines 'C.2.4. 64+36+9. c. 5' and 'C.3. c. 2.' complete the entry for 109 from the previous page.
In the 149 entry, 'C.3.11' and 'C.5.9' are written with the class pairs (the manuscript has 'C.3.11.c' and 'C.5.9 c'); class labels throughout are 'Cl.'/'C.' with paired inverse classes.
In the 157 entry, the line 'C.1.5.c' appears in the image as 'Cl. 1. 5. c'; the transcription 'C. 1. 5. c' is fine.
